lead: In a flotilla the lead crew gives you the forecast every morning, but the decision to reef, to wait or to move the boat is still yours. Learn to read a forecast, the barometer and the local winds of the Ionian and the Aegean.

sections.title: Where the forecast comes from, and which one to trust

blocks.p: Your first source is the lead crew's morning briefing. On your own, the **official forecast** comes from the national met service: coast stations read it on VHF at set times, **NAVTEX** prints it aboard, and harbour offices post it. A warning is announced on channel 16 with the word SÉCURITÉ and read out on a working channel: switch to the channel given, listen, then go back to 16.

fig.note: The text is read on the working channel named

blocks.p: A phone app shows raw model output and misses local effects. Plan on the official forecast and its warnings; when two forecasts disagree, plan on the worse one.

sections.title: Beaufort force, and the gusts on top

blocks.p: Forecasts give the wind as a **Beaufort force**, named from the mean speed. For a charter yacht with a holiday crew, force 4 is a fine sailing day, force 5 wants a reef, and force 7 is a day in harbour.

The force is a mean. **Gusts** run well above it, and they are what overpowers the boat, so set your sails for the gusts. A forecast of 15 knots gusting 25 is force 4 with force 6 in it. Reef in harbour, where it is easy, not outside in the gusts.

A forecast chart joins places of equal pressure with lines called **isobars**. Read their spacing: packed close, the wind is strong; wide apart, it is light. Under a summer high expect little wind, and allow time and fuel for motoring.

Aboard, the **barometer** gives the trend. One reading means little; write it down every few hours. A steady fall of about 1 hPa an hour, with high cloud thickening, says a low is on its way and the wind will rise.

blocks.rule: Close isobars, strong wind. Falling barometer, rising wind.

sections.title: What the land does to the wind

blocks.p: On a hot settled day the land heats up and draws in a **sea breeze** from around midday until evening. It blows onshore, so a calm lunch stop off a beach becomes a **lee shore**. The Ionian's summer northwesterly keeps the same clock: a calm morning, a breeze building from late morning to about force 4, gone around sunset.
High land makes its own wind. At night cold air pours down the valleys in hard gusts, so anchor well clear of a valley mouth.

fig.note: Night gusts come down the valley: B, not A

blocks.p: A wind shift can open your bay to the sea. The wind **veers** when it shifts clockwise, south to west for example, and **backs** when it shifts anticlockwise. Before dark, ask where tonight's wind will come from, and move if the bay will be open to it.

fig.note: South now, veering west: open to the wind

blocks.p: The **Meltemi** blows over the Aegean in summer, hardest in July and August: from the northeast in the north, from the north in the Cyclades, from the northwest in the Dodecanese. It is a fair-weather wind. The sky is clear and the barometer steady while it blows force 6 to 7, so the sky gives no warning. Only the forecast does.

What to expect

blocks.p: If a leg must be made, leave at first light and be in by midday. Do not count on it blowing itself out overnight: plan on the forecast, keep to sheltered legs or stay put, and ask the lead crew for a route.

The forecast is half of the decision; your boat and crew are the other half. Weigh the wind with its gusts, its direction (upwind is slower, wetter and harder), the hours the leg will take and what your crew can stand. A leg to windward takes far longer than its miles suggest: you tack, and the sea slows you. If the answer is doubtful, stay: nobody regrets a day in harbour.

fig.title: Go or no-go?
lines: Force and gusts: within your limit?
Upwind or downwind? How many hours?
Shelter on the way if it gets worse?

blocks.p: **Thunderstorms** are the exception to a quiet forecast. A tall dark cloud building over the land in the afternoon, then thunder, means a sudden violent squall. Reef or drop the sails before it reaches you, not when it hits.

blocks.rule: Reduce sail before the wind arrives. If you wonder whether to reef, reef.
